items.name: narration_en
items.direction: Narrate this as a high-energy, feel-good countdown geography video for BHUGOL, a popular geography fun-facts YouTube channel: the five tiniest, most fake-looking borders on Earth. The Narrator is thrilled to be telling you this: enthusiastic, upbeat, bright and very expressive, like an excited friend who can't wait to show you something amazing. Big smile in the voice the whole way. Wide, lively pitch movement: punch each 'Number five', 'Number four'... like a game-show reveal, rise with real curiosity on every question, give a tiny comic pause before each punchline ('Twice.', 'Swiss league.', 'Belgian again.'), and say every number with genuine amazement. Chars voices two funny cartoon characters, short and punchy. The first line 'Stop trusting your map.' is a bold, playful command. The last line 'Still trust your map?' is a teasing question, voice staying up, so it can loop straight back into the first line. Pace is quick and bouncy, about 170 words per minute, with short crisp pauses; never slow, flat, calm, sleepy or documentary-serious. Accent: native General American English narrator, neutral American accent from the first word to the last. VOICE IDENTITY: always the same warm baritone host, same person and same energy level from the first line to the last. Read numbers naturally. Pronounce 'Büsingen' as 'BOO-zing-en', 'Baarle' as 'BAR-luh', 'Point Roberts' normally. 'Hallo? Germany?' is said in a lost, plaintive little German accent. 'Hola! I mean... bonjour!' is a flustered island correcting itself: bright Spanish 'Hola!', tiny panicked pause, then a sheepish French 'bonjour!'.
lines: These five borders look fake. They're all real.
And number one runs straight through people's homes.
It's in the USA. But the only road in runs through Canada.
So older kids cross the border four times a day. Just for school.
A German village... completely surrounded by Switzerland.
They mostly pay in Swiss francs. Their football team? Swiss league.
Number three: a railway that became a country.
After World War One, Belgium got this German railway. Tracks, land and all.
That thin strip of Belgium cut off five pieces of Germany.
One of them? Just one house and its garden.
Number two: an island that switches country every six months.
Spain runs it half the year. France runs the other half.
They've swapped it for 120 years. And the island? Smaller than a football pitch.
Here, 22 pieces of Belgium are scattered inside the Netherlands.
And some have bits of the Netherlands inside them.
The border runs through shops, cafés... even houses.
So which country do you live in? Wherever your front door is.
When a survey moved the line, one woman's house turned Dutch.
So they moved her front door. Belgian again.
